opus-5.5.text:
I think the final round was less about whether I could solve a tricky algorithm puzzle and more about whether I could build something real, end to end, under time pressure, and have it actually work.

The task was open-ended. You get a fairly loose spec, and it's up to you how you structure it. What I tried to show was the habit I'd built up working on projects like Tianshou and EnvPool: get a minimal version running first, make sure it's correct, then iterate. A lot of people try to design the perfect architecture upfront and run out of time. I'd rather have something ugly that works in the first stretch, and then clean it up, add tests, and optimize once I can see where the bottlenecks are.

The other thing was speed of debugging. When something broke, I didn't panic or start rewriting things randomly. I'd isolate it, print what I needed, check my assumptions, and move on. That only comes from having written and broken a lot of code. With EnvPool, for example, I spent a huge amount of time chasing performance issues and weird concurrency bugs, and that trains a kind of intuition for where problems usually hide.

I also tried to talk through my trade-offs: why I chose a simpler data structure here, why I didn't over-engineer that part. In real research engineering, especially in RL infrastructure, you constantly make those calls. Good engineering isn't writing the cleverest code; it's making the right compromises so the system is fast, correct, and easy for other people to use.

So if I demonstrated anything, I hope it was that: not just raw coding ability, but the practical judgment of someone who has shipped things other people depend on.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think a single final-round task can fully demonstrate anyone's engineering ability, and I'd be a little suspicious of anyone who claims otherwise. What it can show is how you think under constraints.

For me, the thing I tried to do was resist the urge to start coding immediately. I spent the first chunk of time just reading the problem carefully, writing down the invariants, and figuring out which parts were actually hard versus which parts just looked hard. A lot of these tasks are designed so that the obvious approach works for the sample inputs and then falls apart at scale, so I wanted to know where the trap was before I stepped in it.

Then I tried to get a correct, boring version working end to end before optimizing anything. That sounds obvious, but under time pressure people skip it, and then they're debugging a clever solution with no baseline to compare against. Having the slow version gave me a way to verify the fast one on random inputs, which caught a real off-by-one that I would otherwise have shipped.

So if anything, I think what it showed was less about raw cleverness and more about discipline: knowing what to verify, when to simplify, and being honest with myself about what I actually understood versus what I was hoping was true. That's the part that transfers to real engineering, where the problems are messier and nobody hands you a test harness.
